proof:
# Arithmetic radial densities and failure of a convex radial shadow

The radial identities below retain the TRUE mixed centroid and every
through-centroid ambient cap. A subsequent exact example rules out one
natural convexification mechanism; it does not refute the conditional
centroid bound or OC.

## 1. Exact radial formulas

Let C be a convex body in R x R^d, d>=1, whose true mixed-volume centroid
is (0,0). Suppose its mixed d-volume is positive, and write K_z=C_z.
The centroid belongs to C, so (0,0) belongs to C. For each positive integer
k with a nonempty corresponding fiber, set

    Q_k^+=K_k/k,       Q_k^-=-K_(-k)/k.

Empty fibers contribute empty sets. Convexity with the origin gives
Q_(k+1)^+ subset Q_k^+, and likewise on the negative side. Define

 f_+(s)=sum_(k>=1) k^d 1_(Q_k^+)(s),
 g_+(s)=sum_(k>=1) k^(d+1)1_(Q_k^+)(s),             (1)

and similarly f_-,g_-. All sums are finite. A closed through-zero cap
H={a z+u.x>=0} has EXACT mixed mass

 |K_0 cap {u.x>=0}|
 +integral_(a+u.s>=0) f_+(s)ds
 +integral_(a+u.s<=0) f_-(s)ds.                    (2)

Indeed positive points are (k,ks), negative ones (-k,-ks), and the Jacobian
in each continuous fiber is k^d. This proof retains equality signs,
including the vertical caps for which the central fiber is boundary mass.
Zero d-volume fibers cause no extra terms in these integrals.

The TRUE integer and continuous centroid equations become

    integral g_+ = integral g_-,
    integral s(g_+-g_-)ds+integral_(K_0) x dx=0.    (3)

Let R_+(s)=sup{r>=0:(r,rs) belongs to C}, and define R_- using (-r,-rs).
Each intersection with the ray is the interval from zero to R_+(s),
possibly just zero. Therefore, with m_+(s)=floor R_+(s),

 f_+(s)=F_d(m_+(s)), g_+(s)=F_(d+1)(m_+(s)),
 F_p(m)=sum_(k=1)^m k^p.                            (4)

The same holds negatively. If the gauge of C is infinite in a direction,
use R=0 there; otherwise R=1/rho_C(+/-1,+/-s). No interior-origin gauge
assumption is needed for the ray-interval statement. At an exact integer
radius the last fiber point belongs to the closed body and is included.

There is an exact scalar relation between the two radial densities. Let
Phi_d be the continuous piecewise-affine function joining

    (F_d(m),F_(d+1)(m)), m=0,1,2,... .

Its slope on [F_d(m-1),F_d(m)] is m, so Phi_d is increasing and convex,
and g_+=Phi_d(f_+), g_-=Phi_d(f_-) pointwise. Consequently for any measurable
set E of finite positive measure,

    integral_E g_+ >= |E| Phi_d((integral_E f_+)/|E|), (5)

and the analogous negative-side bound. This is ordinary Jensen; equality
is attained on every single radial plateau. These formulas alone do not
replace the geometric compatibility of the two ray families.

## 2. The natural angular-volume radial shadow need not be convex

Already for n=d=1 take the rectangle

    C=[-3,3]x[-1,1].

Its seven integer fibers all have length two, and its true mixed centroid
is exactly (0,0) by central symmetry. In the positive projective chart
(z,x)=r(1,s),

    R(s)=min(3,1/|s|),
    f_+(s)=sum_(1<=k<=R(s)) k.                     (6)

The coordinate Jacobian is r. Hence a planar radial body with radius
R_hat(s) has angular area density R_hat(s)^2/2 in this chart. Matching the
positive noncentral mixed cap density in (2) would require

    R_hat(s)=sqrt(2f_+(s))                           (7)

almost everywhere. This matching uses ambient area only as an auxiliary
shadow construction; it does not change the original mixed measure.

The gauge 1/R_hat(s) is constant at one value on each of the open intervals
(1/2,1) and (1/3,1/2), and has different limits at s=1/2. Both intervals
lie in the interior of the positive cone generated by the rectangle.
A finite convex gauge is continuous on the interior of its domain. Thus
no convex radial body can realize (7), even if its values on the finitely
many angular boundaries are changed. This is an almost-everywhere
obstruction, not a choice of values on a zero-measure boundary.

There is a stronger obstruction to trying to repair this merely by
continuous arithmetic interpolation at integer radii. At the exact knots
s=1,1/2,1/3, the arithmetic radius rule prescribes gauge values

    psi(1)=1/sqrt(2),
    psi(1/2)=1/sqrt(6),
    psi(1/3)=1/sqrt(12).

Since 1/2=(1/4)1+(3/4)(1/3), convexity of ANY such gauge would require

    1/sqrt(6)<=1/(4sqrt(2))+3/(4sqrt(12)).           (8)

The inequality is strictly reversed. After multiplying by 4sqrt(12),
the strict reverse reads 4sqrt(2)>sqrt(6)+3. Squaring reduces it to
17>6sqrt(6), whose square is the integer inequality 289>216; all quantities
being squared are positive. Thus even a continuous interpolation matching
those three arithmetic knots cannot be convex. This interpolation test
is a separate specified requirement, not an assertion that preservation
of angular measure forces values at isolated knots.

For d=1 the polynomial interpolation of the power sum makes the failure
especially transparent: F_1(R)=R(R+1)/2 would give, on a chart where
rho_C(1,s)=s>0,

    psi(s)=s/sqrt(1+s),
    psi''(s)=-(1+s/4)/(1+s)^(5/2)<0.

The exact discrete arithmetic data therefore do not become a convex gauge
under this natural interpolation. This differs from the previously proved
concavity of F_d(m)^(1/(d+1)) in the INTEGER argument m; projective reciprocal
coordinates impose a different inequality.

The central-fiber term in (2) remains separate throughout. The local
positive-chart contradiction in (8) persists even if an attempted shadow
adds other directions to account for that term. It cannot be fixed by
filling only missing angular regions while retaining the displayed knots.
The rectangle itself has maximum and centroid depth 1/2, so none of these
obstructions is a bad-depth example for the original problem.
